sections.html:
Wentzville sits in western St. Charles County. The city counted 44,372 people in 2020 and now has about 49,495, up from 29,070 in 2010. That growth shows in the housing: owners live in 82.5% of homes, the median owner-reported home value is $331,300, median rent is $1,345, and median household income is $112,394. The average commute is 27.8 minutes, so many buyers are weighing the drive to St. Louis jobs.

Wentzville does not inspect a house just because it changes hands. Renting is where the city steps in. Below you will find the inspection rules, the small fees buyers ask about, the county tax calendar and a short prep list.

An ordinary sale needs no inspection. The city asks for one only when a house is going to be leased, and the house must pass it before a tenant takes the keys. A buyer who will live there never deals with this.

  • The residential occupancy inspection costs $50 and stays valid for 90 days.
  • Request it through the city's SmartGov permit portal. Once the fee is paid, scheduling normally takes one to two business days.
  • Every change of resident at a property means a fresh inspection.
  • A buyer of new construction does not need one, because the builder gets occupancy with the construction permit.

Questions go to the Building Division at (636) 327-5101, open weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. An investor buyer who intends to rent should hear about the 90-day window early, so the tenant's start date holds.

sections.h2: City and county fees at a glance
sections.html:
Buyers and tenants tend to ask about these dollar amounts.

Fees tied to a Wentzville house
FeeAmountWhen it applies
Residential occupancy inspection$50Rental or lease, valid 90 days
Water, trash and sewer account deposit$150New service at the address
Partial property tax paymentFrom $20Paid to the county Collector
E-check payment of tax$1.50Online or by phone
Card payment of taxAbout 2.5 percentOnline or by phone

The city keeps the $150 deposit until the account shows two years of good payment, then credits it back. New owners see this charge, so tell them before they are surprised.

You have three basic choices: list with an agent, sell it yourself, or take an investor's offer. The city puts no hurdle in front of any of them for an owner-occupied sale, so the choice comes down to speed, cost and how the house looks today.

  • Agent listing. Ask for the commission rate in writing, plus an estimate of repair and staging costs.
  • Sale by owner. You price it and show it yourself, and a title company still closes it.
  • Investor offer. An investor may buy the house in its present shape. If that investor will rent it out, the $50 occupancy inspection comes before any tenant.

Before comparing offers, total up your debts against the house. Any mortgage, home equity line or overdue property tax comes out of the sale proceeds, and each lender can send a payoff statement.

sections.h2: Property tax: who bills it and how to pay
sections.html:
The county, not the city, sends Wentzville's property tax bill. Go to the Collector of Revenue at 201 N. Second Street, Suite 134, in St. Charles, or call 636-949-7470. You can pay in installments starting at $20, but part-payment does not pull a parcel off the tax certificate sale list.

  • Paying by e-check, online or by phone, costs $1.50. Cards run about 2.5 percent.
  • A mailed check counts as of its USPS postmark. Dropping it in the mail on December 31 can mean a postmark the next business day.
  • If you use your bank's bill-pay, schedule it at least five working days ahead of December 31. The county goes by the day the money arrives.

A value you think is too high goes first to an informal hearing with the Assessor's Office, held from late April into early June. In a year without reassessment, call 636-949-7428 to set one up. Still unhappy? File with the Board of Equalization, whose form is due at 5 p.m. on the second Monday of July every year.

The final step is the Missouri State Tax Commission. You file by September 30, or 30 days after the Board rules if that is later, and a buyer who bought after the second Monday in June has until December 31. Your assessment notice prints the full instructions, so keep it close.

You can still sell with an overdue county bill. The title company requests the amount from the Collector and takes it out of what you receive at the table. If you can, settle it sooner, since part-payment leaves the parcel exposed to the certificate sale. A call to the Collector gets you today's figure before you say yes to an offer.

sections.h2: What to gather before you list
sections.html:
Gather the paperwork first: loan payoff, latest county tax bill, HOA dues if any, and a list of repairs you have made lately. After that, decide what cleaning and fixing is worth paying for before the first showing.

To avoid a long listing period, collect written investor offers and set each one against a realistic list price minus agent fees, repairs and carrying costs. Read who pays closing costs and what happens if the buyer backs out.

A cash sale to an investor skips the showings, the repair negotiations and most of the waiting on a buyer's loan, but it only makes sense if the net figure beats what a listing would leave you after fees and repairs.

After you accept an offer, the title company runs a lien search and drafts the settlement statement. Loan payoffs and any back tax are subtracted from the price, and you keep what is left. Wentzville adds no city paperwork to an owner-occupied sale, so closing here looks like closing anywhere else in the county.

If the buyer will rent the house afterward, the occupancy inspection is theirs to schedule, but it helps if you leave the house accessible and utilities on so an inspector can walk through. For a buyer who is moving in, the main city task is opening the water, trash and sewer account, which is where the deposit comes in.

Bring the title company your photo ID, the loan account number and the latest tax statement. Ask what time keys and garage openers must be handed over and whether the buyer will want a final walk-through the day before.

faqs.q: Does Wentzville inspect a house before it is sold?
faqs.a: No. The city requires no occupancy inspection when a house is sold. An inspection applies only when the house will be leased or rented to a new tenant.

faqs.q: How much is the Wentzville occupancy inspection?
faqs.a: It costs $50 and is valid for 90 days. You request it through the SmartGov permit portal, and scheduling usually takes one to two business days after payment.

faqs.q: Which county bills Wentzville property tax?
faqs.a: St. Charles County does. The Collector of Revenue is at 201 N. Second Street, Suite 134, in St. Charles, and can be reached at 636-949-7470.

faqs.q: When is the assessment appeal deadline in Wentzville?
faqs.a: The Board of Equalization form is due by 5 p.m. on the second Monday in July each year. A later State Tax Commission appeal generally needs a Board filing first, unless the property was newly purchased.

faqs.q: How big is the Wentzville market?
faqs.a: About 49,495 people live in Wentzville, up from 44,372 in 2020, in western St. Charles County. Owners live in 82.5% of homes.
